## Where we are

- $F_{IS}$ (deck 02) measured a **heterozygote deficit within a deme**. The biggest cause
  in plants is the **mating system**.
- Plants run the full gamut: obligate outcrossers, mixed maters, near-complete selfers,
  clonal spreaders, and asexual (apomictic) seed producers.
- **Today:** how mating system rewrites genotype frequencies, and how we read it off the
  genome. *(Computer Activity 1 follows.)*

## Learning objectives

By the end you should be able to:

- Define the **inbreeding coefficient $F$** as a probability of identity by descent (IBD).
- Relate $F$ to **kinship** via $r_0, r_1, r_2$.
- Predict genotype frequencies and heterozygosity under inbreeding.
- Derive the **equilibrium $F$ under partial selfing**, $F = s/(2-s)$.
- Recognize genomic signatures of **clonality and apomixis**.

# Identity by descent {.center}

## Relatedness and IBD

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- Every pair of individuals is connected by a **pedigree**; closer relatives are separated
  by **fewer meioses** and so share more genome.
- Two alleles are **identical by descent (IBD)** if inherited from a recent common
  ancestor (ignoring mutation).
- IBD is the currency of inbreeding, kinship, and (later) heritability.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

chromosomes colored, an IBD block persisting across a long stretch.

## Kinship from IBD probabilities

For two outbred individuals $i,j$, let $r_0, r_1, r_2$ be the probabilities they share
$0,1,2$ alleles IBD at a locus. The **coefficient of kinship** $F_{ij}$ is the probability
that one random allele from each are IBD:

$$
F_{ij} = 0\cdot r_0 + \tfrac14 r_1 + \tfrac12 r_2 .
$$

| Relationship | $r_0$ | $r_1$ | $r_2$ | $F_{ij}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| parent–child | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1/4 |
| full siblings | 1/4 | 1/2 | 1/4 | 1/4 |
| monozygotic / clonemates | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1/2 |
| first cousins | 3/4 | 1/4 | 0 | 1/16 |

::: {.notes}
The $\tfrac14 r_1$ comes from needing to draw the one shared allele from *both* individuals
($\tfrac12\times\tfrac12$). Clonemates ($r_2=1$) sit at the top — important for apomicts.
:::

# Inbreeding {.center}

## Genotype frequencies under inbreeding

With inbreeding coefficient $F$ (the probability an individual's two alleles are IBD), mix
the IBD case (frequency $F$, always homozygous) with the random-union case (frequency
$1-F$, HW):

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 & A_1A_1 & A_1A_2 & A_2A_2 \\ \hline
\text{freq} & p^2 + Fpq & 2pq(1-F) & q^2 + Fpq
\end{array}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow\quad H = 2pq(1-F), \qquad F = 1 - \frac{H_{\text{obs}}}{H_{\text{exp}}} .
$$

- $F$ shifts mass from heterozygotes to homozygotes **without changing allele frequencies**.
- This is exactly $F_{IS}$ from deck 02, now read as an IBD probability.

## Selfing drives $F$ upward

Under **complete selfing**, a heterozygote's offspring are heterozygous only half the
time; homozygotes stay homozygous. The IBD probability updates as

$$
F_{t+1} = \tfrac12(1) + \tfrac12 F_t = \frac{1 + F_t}{2} \;\longrightarrow\; 1 .
$$

. . .

Under **partial selfing** at rate $s$ (outcrossing $1-s$), IBD is created only in the
selfed fraction:

$$
F_{t+1} = s\left(\frac{1 + F_t}{2}\right) + (1-s)\cdot 0 .
$$

## Equilibrium inbreeding under partial selfing

Set $F_{t+1} = F_t = \hat F$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat F &= \frac{s}{2}\left(1 + \hat F\right) \\[4pt]
\hat F\left(1 - \tfrac{s}{2}\right) &= \frac{s}{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\boxed{\;\hat F = \frac{s}{2 - s}\;}
\end{aligned}
$$

| $s$ | 0 | 0.5 | 0.9 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\hat F$ | 0 | 1/3 | 0.82 | 1 |

- Selfing rate maps directly onto an **expected heterozygosity deficit**.

## Worked example — *Capsella*

***Capsella grandiflora*** is an obligate outcrosser ($s\approx 0$); its sister
***C. rubella*** shifted to **selfing** within the last ~50–100 kya
[@foxe2009capsella; @slotte2013capsella].

- Outcrosser: $\hat F \approx 0$, heterozygosity near the HW expectation.
- Selfer ($s \approx 0.9$): $\hat F = \dfrac{0.9}{2 - 0.9} \approx 0.82$ — most loci
  homozygous, diversity and $N_e$ collapsed.

::: {.callout-note}
The selfing transition is the single most consequential mating-system shift in plants — it
reshapes diversity, LD, and the efficacy of selection genome-wide.
:::

## Consequences of selfing

- **Heterozygosity** $\downarrow$ (by factor $1-F$); **effective recombination**
  $\downarrow$ (rare heterozygotes ⟹ crossovers do nothing) ⟹ genome-wide **LD** $\uparrow$.
- **$N_e$** $\downarrow$ (toward half the outcrossing value), lowering diversity and the
  efficacy of selection (linked selection reaches further).
- **Purging** of recessive load; the **"selfing syndrome"** (smaller, less showy flowers,
  reduced herkogamy).

<span class="xref">→ reduced diversity feeds directly into the SFS/Tajima's $D$ signatures
of deck 04.</span>

# Avoiding selfing {.center}

## Self-incompatibility and heterostyly

Many plants **enforce outcrossing** — the mirror image of selfing, and a genomic signature
in its own right.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}
- **Self-incompatibility (SI):** the **S-locus** rejects self (and matching) pollen —
  *gametophytic* (pollen's own haploid $S$ allele) or *sporophytic* (parent diploid genotype).
- SI is a textbook **disassortable / balancing-selection** system: rare $S$-haplotypes mate
  more, so selection maintains **many long-lived alleles** at **excess heterozygosity** —
  the plant analog of the fungal mating-type example.
- **Heterostyly** (distyly in *Primula*, Darwin) — a morphological outcrossing switch
  (pin/thrum) controlled by a linked supergene.
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}

diagram; optionally the S-allele frequency spectrum (many balanced alleles).

# Clonality and apomixis {.center}

## When sex is rare or absent

Many plants reproduce **clonally** (rhizomes, ramets) or via **apomixis** (asexual seed).
Genomic signatures differ sharply from selfing:

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Identical multilocus genotypes (MLGs)** repeated across "individuals" (ramets).
- **Fixed / excess heterozygosity** — no segregation to break heterozygotes up
  ($r_2 \to 1$, the clonemate row above).
- **Meselson effect** — the two alleles at a locus diverge over time without
  recombination.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}
**FIGURE** — clonal vs. sexual signature: an MLG histogram with tall repeated genotypes,
or a map of identical ramets (e.g. *Populus* "Pando", *Taraxacum*, *Boechera*).
:::

## Estimating the mating system

- Estimate selfing rate $s$ from the heterozygote deficit ($\hat F = s/(2-s)$) or from
  **multilocus** methods (e.g. RMES, progeny-array $t$).
- **Identity disequilibrium** — correlated heterozygosity across loci — distinguishes
  selfing from other causes of a heterozygote deficit (e.g. null alleles, Wahlund).
- *Computer Activity 1:* estimate $F$ / $s$ from a genotype matrix and interpret it.

# Computer Activity 1 — life history & diversity {.center}

## Simulating diversity with `msprime`

We'll simulate samples under the **coalescent** and watch how **life history reshapes
diversity**. Selfing's main population-genetic effects are to **lower $N_e$** (toward half)
and to **collapse effective recombination** — we encode both as rescaled parameters.

```python
import msprime, numpy as np

def diversity_sim(Ne, recomb, mu=1e-8, L=1e6, n=50, seed=1):
    ts = msprime.sim_ancestry(samples=n, population_size=Ne,
                              recombination_rate=recomb, sequence_length=L,
                              random_seed=seed)
    ts = msprime.sim_mutations(ts, rate=mu, random_seed=seed)
    pi  = ts.diversity()                      # nucleotide diversity (per site)
    sfs = ts.allele_frequency_spectrum(polarised=True, span_normalise=False)
    return pi, sfs
```

::: {.notes}
Display-only; to run live, change ```` ```python ```` to ```` ```{python} ```` (needs the
jupyter engine + `pip install msprime tskit`). msprime is a coalescent simulator, so we
mimic selfing by rescaling Ne and the recombination rate rather than modeling selfing
explicitly.
:::

## Outcrosser vs. selfer

```python
# Outcrosser: full Ne, normal recombination
pi_out, sfs_out = diversity_sim(Ne=10000, recomb=1e-8)
# Selfer: ~half Ne, recombination effectively crushed
pi_self, sfs_self = diversity_sim(Ne=5000,  recomb=1e-10)

print(round(pi_out, 5), round(pi_self, 5))   # selfer << outcrosser
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Predict, then check:**

- Which has higher $\pi$ and $\theta_W$?
- How does the **SFS shape** differ (rare vs. intermediate)?
- Vary the selfing rate $s$ and relate $N_e$ back to $\hat F = s/(2-s)$.
:::

## Summary — key equations

$$
F_{ij} = \tfrac14 r_1 + \tfrac12 r_2
\qquad
H = 2pq(1-F)
\qquad
\hat F = \frac{s}{2-s}
$$

- Inbreeding $=$ IBD; the mating system sets its level.
- **Selfing** inflates $F$ to $s/(2-s)$, crushing heterozygosity, recombination, and $N_e$.
- **Clonality/apomixis** leave repeated MLGs and excess heterozygosity — the opposite
  fingerprint.
